lesson.title: Measuring Angles by Arc Length: Why Calculus Prefers Radians
lesson.summary: This section defines the radian as an angle measure based on arc length along the unit circle, gives the conversion between degrees and radians, and explains why radians rather than degrees are the natural unit for calculus.
lesson.body:
Degrees divide a circle into 360 equal pieces, a convention with ancient roots but no deep mathematical necessity behind the specific number 360. Radians measure angles a completely different way, tied directly to the unit circle. One radian is defined as the angle that, when its ray sweeps counterclockwise starting from the positive x-axis, traces out an arc along the unit circle exactly 1 unit long. Because the unit circle has radius 1, this means the numerical value of an angle in radians is literally the length of the arc it cuts out on that circle, arc length and angle measure become the same number.

Since the full circumference of a circle with radius r is 2*pi*r, the unit circle, with r = 1, has circumference 2*pi. A full 360° rotation therefore traces out an arc of length 2*pi, meaning 360° = 2*pi radians. Dividing both sides by 2 gives the single most useful conversion fact: 180° = pi radians. From this, converting between the two systems is a matter of multiplication: to convert degrees to radians, multiply by pi/180; to convert radians to degrees, multiply by 180/pi.

Converting 45° to radians: 45 * (pi/180) = 45pi/180 = pi/4. Converting the other direction, take 5pi/6 radians to degrees: (5pi/6) * (180/pi) = (5*180)/6 = 900/6 = 150°. This matches the 150° angle used earlier on the unit circle, where cos(150°) = -sqrt(3)/2 and sin(150°) = 1/2, confirming that 5pi/6 radians and 150° describe the exact same position on the circle.

For a circle of any radius r, not just the unit circle, the arc length formula generalizes to s = r*theta, but only when theta is measured in radians, which is precisely why the radian was defined the way it was. As a concrete example, a circle with radius 4 and a central angle of 2pi/3 radians has an arc length of s = 4 * (2pi/3) = 8pi/3, which is approximately 8.378 units. Trying to use this same simple formula with theta measured in degrees would require an extra conversion factor, since degrees were never tied to arc length in the first place.

This arc length connection is not just a convenience, it is the reason radians become the required unit once calculus formulas for sine and cosine are introduced. The clean derivative rules, such as the derivative of sin(x) being cos(x), only hold exactly when x is measured in radians, because those rules are derived from limits that depend on the arc-length definition established here. Working in degrees introduces an extra constant factor of pi/180 into every derivative, cluttering formulas that are otherwise remarkably simple, which is why every calculus course from this point forward measures angles in radians by default.
